Introduction 36

Cereblon (CRBN) is a substrate recognition adapter of the CRL4CRBN E3 ubiquitin ligase complex 37

that mediates protein selection for ubiquitination and degradation. CRBN was first described in 38

association with neurological development in humans1 and subsequently identified as a primary 39

target of thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide, ligands that bind to the conserved 40

thalidomide-binding domain (TBD) of CRBN2,3 (Figure 1a–c). Induced substrate degradation 41

partially underlies the observed therapeutic efficacy of thalidomide and its derivatives in multiple 42

myeloma4,5 and del(5q) myelodysplastic syndrome,6 as well as off-target teratogenic effects.7-9 43

These findings have sparked immense efforts in the field of targeted protein degradation to induce 44

a range of substrates to CRBN for therapeutic benefit.10,11 By contrast, the endogenous substrates 45

mediated by CRBN and how they are affected by thalidomide and its derivatives remain relatively 46

underexplored. 47

Studies on the physiological function of CRBN have begun to reveal the molecular determinants 48

for endogenous substrate recognition through the TBD. Our investigation of endogenous chemical 49

motifs that thalidomide mimics led to the identification of the C-terminal cyclic imide modification 50

that constitutes the minimal recognition motif, or degron, used by CRBN to recognize and remove 51

substrates (Figure 1b–e).12 Coincident efforts provided a structural basis for C-terminal cyclic 52

imide binding to the TBD.13 The C-terminal cyclic imide primarily arises from cyclization of 53

asparagine, wherein the side chain amide attacks the carbonyl in the protein backbone, leading 54

to generation of the C-terminal aspartimide (cN, Figure 1f). This modification can be formed as a 55

result of intramolecular cleavage of the protein backbone during protein aging or stress, as occurs 56

on glutathione synthetase (GSS),14 or via an enzymatic pathway for conversion of the C-terminal 57

asparagine residue of proteins by protein carboxymethyltransferase (PCMT1) that go on to 58

become substrates for CRBN (Figure 1g).15 The latter emerging pathway wherein PCMT1 acts 59

on C-terminal asparagine to promote cyclic imide formation provides a molecular basis for prior 60

studies on endogenous substrates that interface with the TBD, such as glutamine synthetase 61

(GLUL).15,16 Thus, further investigation of the regulation of substrates by PCMT1 and CRBN 62

through the C-terminal cyclic imide may illuminate deleterious effects on the brain and other 63

phenotypes resulting from loss-of-function of PCMT1, CRBN, or their substrates, as well as their 64

contribution to desirable or undesirable effects of thalidomide and its derivatives. 65

A generalizable method to visualize endogenous CRBN substrates that bear the C-terminal cyclic 66

imide modification is critical to accelerate these investigations. However, methods for detecting 67

C-terminal cyclic imides are currently confined to mass spectrometry analyses. Typically, the C- 68

terminal cyclic imide can be detected by searching global proteomics datasets for semitryptic 69

peptides with a dehydrated C-terminal asparagine or glutamine residue.12,14 However, these 70

modifications may occur on peptides that are not ideal for trypsin digestion, the analyses must be 71

controlled for mass spectrometry artifacts,17 and sensitivity is likely impacted by detection limits 72

in the absence of an enrichment method. Furthermore, the C-terminal cyclic imide is prone to 73

hydrolysis with a protein half-life of approximately 24 h,12 which can be lost during lengthy 74

preparation protocols. Hydrolysis of the cyclic imide is further accelerated by basic conditions, 75

such as those typically used in sample preparation for global proteomics experiments.14 By 76

contrast, analyses of many protein modifications have been dramatically accelerated by 77

modification-specific antibodies to detect, enrich, or image the modification in the proteome.18 We 78

therefore sought to develop an antibody-like reagent for C-terminal cyclic imides to accelerate the 79

study of this overlooked modification on endogenous substrates of CRBN. 80

In defining criteria for our antibody-like reagent, we considered the features of successful 81

antibodies: good binding affinity to our epitope (KD under 1 M), stability in Western blot and 82

enrichment experimental conditions, a slow off-rate with the C-terminal cyclic imide to maintain 83

interactions through washing steps, the feasible ability to obtain sufficient quantities, and 84

compatibility with other commercially available reagents. Furthermore, a C-terminal cyclic imide 85

Results 99

Development of cerebody by protein engineering 100

To begin engineering a known C-terminal cyclic imide binder into a suitable tool for detecting 101

CRBN substrates, we first considered a series of CRBN constructs for their ability to be turned 102

into a method for detection of CRBN substrates (Figure 2a). CRBN alone is unstable but is readily 103

expressed in complex with DDB1, which has previously been used for affinity enrichment 104

procedures to identify induced substrates of thalidomide derivatives.4 The CRBN/DDB1 complex 105

has a good basal affinity to C-terminal cyclic imides, with a KD, CRBN/DDB1 = 96 +/– 21 nM to 106

thalidomide-FITC (thal-FITC) by time-resolved Forster resonance energy transfer (TR-FRET) 107

(Figure 2b, Extended Data Figure 1a), but is recombinantly expressed in insect cells and is 108

unstable to E. coli overexpression, making it relatively challenging to readily obtain in large 109

quantity. The TBD alone has a lower basal affinity to C-terminal cyclic imides, with KD, TBD = 253 110

We next investigated the TBD of CRBN, which has a relatively weak but measurable KD to C- 136

terminal cyclic imides and can be overexpressed in E. coli in scalable amounts (around 2 mg/L). 137

Indeed, comparison of the binding of a thal–FITC probe to either CRBN/DDB1 or the TBD showed 138

an approximate 2.5-fold difference between the constructs, which is within the range of binding 139

affinity that could be recovered by directed evolution.26 We therefore considered the TBD as a 140

good candidate for an affinity maturation campaign performed by random mutagenesis with a 141

phage display library. We created a library of TBD derivatives with random mutations at a 142

frequency of 9 mutations/kb fused to the N-terminus of pIII of filamentous phage.27 Phage were 143

selected by in solution affinity to GFP-LcN, GFP-LcQ, GFP-FcN, GFP-FcQ, or GFP-PcQ 144

(Extended Data Figure 1e). Mutations appearing at a variant frequency above 10% in the third 145

and fourth rounds of selection were considered for validation, with preference given to variants 146

that appeared in multiple selection conditions (Supplemental Tables 1–3). We individually 147

overexpressed and purified hits selected for validation. Each TBD mutant was labeled with 148

CoraFluor-128 and examined for binding affinity to thal-FITC by TR-FRET. While calculated KD 149

values varied across experimental preparations, trends of constructs’ relative binding affinities 150

remained largely consistent across experiments. For the first round, we selected 11 hits to 151

characterize and found that the P424A mutation improved binding affinity to thal-FITC 152

(Supplemental Table 4). A second round of phage display on a library based on TBD P424A 153

yielded nine double mutants that were examined, with the double mutant A395T/P424A showing 154

the strongest improvement in binding affinity to thal-FITC (Supplemental Table 4). A third round 155

of phage display with a library based on TBD A395T/P424A did not produce any mutations at a 156

variant frequency above 10%, and examination of six triple mutant TBD derivatives with a variant 157

frequency between 5 and 10% did not yield a derivative that further enhanced the binding affinity 158

(Supplemental Table 4). These efforts thus resulted in the identification of the double mutant 159

TBD A395T/P424A with an approximately 2-fold improvement in binding affinity, which is at the 160

upper edge of the range that is usable for enrichment.26 161

Detection of CRBN substrates by Western blot 199

We next examined cerebody’s utility as a primary antibody in Western blotting experiments 200

(Figure 3a). We assessed its ability to detect C-terminal cyclic imides on proteins previously 201

demonstrated to be degraded in a CRBN-dependent manner, including GLUL-cN generated by 202

the reaction of recombinant GLUL with PCMT115 or C-terminal cyclic imides installed on GFP12 or 203

GSS14 by eSrtA-catalyzed reactions (Extended Data Figure 4a, Figure 3b-c). Using these 204

protein standards, we examined detection efficiency against serial dilutions of GFP-PFQYKcN, 205

GSS-cN, and GLUL-cN when spiked into HEK293T lysates (Extended Data Figure 4b). We 206

determined that cerebody is best used at a working concentration of 5 M with 5% nonfat dried 207

milk in TBST as the blocking buffer with a HRP-conjugated -HA antibody at 1:1000 dilution in 208

blocking buffer as the secondary antibody (Extended Data Figure 4b). These conditions show a 209

limit of detection between 3.2 x 10–13 and 6.4 x 10–14 mol of protein, comparable to the 210

approximately 10–12 mol limit of detection of antibodies developed for other PTMs30 (Figure 3d). 211

Discussion 320

Here we present the development of cerebody, a robust protein reagent to visualize and enrich 321

CRBN substrates. CRBN and its substrates have been the subject of significant investigation due 322

to their potential to be affected by CRBN-directed targeted protein degradation modalities10,11 and 323

their important yet underexplored role in human biology.1,37 However, CRBN’s principle 324

recognition motif of substrates through a protein modification, the C-terminal cyclic imide degron, 325

has made these substrates challenging to visualize in a routine manner other than by global 326

proteomics. By leveraging protein engineering approaches to derivatize CRBNmidi,23 we now 327

report the development of cerebody as a reagent that renders routine the detection of CRBN 328

substrates. We report the use of cerebody to detect, enrich, and discover proteins with C-terminal 329

cyclic imides including engineered proteins, recombinant proteins, and endogenous CRBN 330

substrates like GLUL and UROD. This method will accelerate the understanding of the native 331

interactors of CRBN, the mechanisms through which they interact to shed light on CRBN’s 332

physiological function, and the ways these pathways are impacted by CRBN ligands. 333

Use of CRBN as an enrichment modality16,38,39 along with a number of emerging technologies 334

using proximity-based labeling have been employed to characterize CRBN interactors, primarily 335


<!-- Page 16 -->


15

in the presence of small molecule ligands.33,40-45 Enrichment with CRBN/DDB1 can be a 336

successful strategy to identify induced substrates and provide insights to endogenous substrates 337

like GLUL,16 but use of this protein complex is relatively constrained by the expression system, 338

not compatible with Western blot, and enrichments can be highly variable in our experience. 339

Proximity-labeling strategies for proteins in proximity to CRBN or following protein ubiquitination 340

in a CRBN-dependent manner are complementary approaches that are revealing profiles which 341

include proteins like GLUL and PPA1 that are likewise observed in our cerebody enrichments.40,42- 342
